1. These petitions are filed for transfer of guardianship petition proceedings in
G.W.O.P. No.1779 of 2022, divorce petition being F.C.O.P No.2083 of 2022 and
Maintenance Petition being M.C. No.440 of 2024 initiated by the respondent-
wife, from Family Court, Hyderabad to Family Court, Mumbai.
2. The parties have entered into a settlement agreement on 25.08.2026. The
terms of the agreement, as agreed to, between the parties, reads as under :
“1. DISSOLUTION OF MARRIAGE BY MUTUAL CONSENT
1.1.  The  marriage  has  broken  down  irretrievably.  The  Parties  have
therefore  mutually  and  freely  agreed  to  dissolve  the  marriage  by
mutual consent in accordance with law, on the terms recorded in this
Deed.
1.2.  The  Transfer  Petitions  are  already  pending  before  the  Hon'ble
Supreme Court. The Parties will therefore jointly file an application in
1

--- Page 39 ---
the Transfer Petitions, place this Deed on record, and pray that the
Hon'ble  Court,  in  exercise  of  its  power  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India:
a) dissolve the marriage by a decree of divorce by mutual consent,
waiving the waiting period under Section 13B(2) of the HMA;
b) take on record the undertakings of the Parties to abide by this Deed;
and
c) dispose of the Pending Proceedings, including the DV Case, in terms
of this settlement.
1.3. For this purpose, the Wife will enter appearance in the Transfer
Petitions  through  counsel  of  her  choice.  Both  Parties  shall  remain
present  before  the  Hon'ble  Court,  in  person  or  through  video-
conference, as and when required.
1.4. If the Hon'ble Supreme Court declines to grant the decree, the
Parties will take every step necessary until a decree is granted.
1.5. Neither Party will withdraw or resile from the consent for divorce,
so long as the other complies with this Deed, and subject to the terms
contained in this Deed.
2. SETTLEMENT AMOUNT AND PAYMENT SCHEDULE
2.1. In place of all separate claims for alimony, maintenance and the
Children's expenses, the Parties have agreed on a single, consolidated
settlement.
2.2. The Husband will pay a total of INR 3,00,00,000/- [Rupees Three

2.2.2.1.INR  1,00,00,000/-  [Rupees  One  Crore  only]  towards

2.2.2.2.  INR  50,00,000/-  [Rupees  Fifty  Lakh  only]  towards
streedhan, jewellery. gifts and dowry articles etc.

following bank account of the Wife:

3. FULL AND FINAL SETTLEMENT
3.1.  This  settlement  is  intended  to  close  every  monetary  and
proprietary  claim  arising  out  of  the  marriage.  Accordingly,  in
consideration of the Settlement Amount, the Wife gives up every
claim, past, present or future, against the Husband and against his
parents,  siblings,  relatives  and  family  members  (including  all
respondents in the DV Case listed in Schedule I). This includes claims
for: (a) maintenance under any law, including Sections 24 and 25 of
the  HMA,  Section  125  of  the  Code  of  Criminal  Procedure,
1973/Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023,
Section  18  of  the  Hindu  Adoptions  and  Maintenance  Act,  1956
["HAMA"], and Sections 18 to 22 of the Protection of Women from
Domestic Violence Act, 2005 [" DV Act"]; (b) alimony; (c) streedhan,
jewellery,  gifts  and  dowry  articles;  (d)  right  of  residence  in  any
shared  household  under  Section  17  of  the  DV  Act;  and  (e)
compensation, damages and costs.
3.2. The amounts to be paid as aforesaid shall also be in full and final
settlement  of  the  Wife's  claim(s),  if  any,  towards  streedhan,
jewellery, gifts and dowry articles etc. The Wife confirms that nothing
further remains due to her on account thereof.
3.3. The Children's rights, if any, in the estate of the Husband are
governed exclusively by Clause 8.6 of this Deed, and no further or
additional right is created by this Clause.
3.4.  The  Husband,  in  consideration  of  the  mutual  settlement
recorded in this Deed, gives up every claim, past, present or future,
against  the  Wife  and  against  her  parents,  siblings,  relatives  and
family members, including any claim for damages, compensation,
costs, return of gifts, or any claim arising out of or in connection with
the marriage, the Pending Proceedings, or the conduct of the Wife or
her family in the course thereof.

not serve any purpose. Hence, the prayer sought for dissolution of marriage,
which  came  to  be  solemnized  on  02.12.2003  between  the  parties  stands
dissolved.  The  disputes  that  are  pending  before  the  various  forums  stand
quashed.

the  settlement  agreement  and  both  the  parties  are  directed  to  bear  their
respective costs.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.

--- Page 66 ---
2
2. The  present  appeals  arise  out  of  judgment  dated
01.11.2023 passed by High Court of Delhi in Writ Petition (C)
No. 13576 of 2023 and batch, thereby setting aside the common
order dated 15.05.2023 of the Central Administrative Tribunal
(in short ‘CAT’) in Original Application No. 3724 of 2022 and
batch, wherein appellants sought directions for consideration
for  appointment  to  the  post  of  ‘Principal’  under  the
Directorate  of  Education,  Government  of  National  Capital
Territory of Delhi in terms of advertisement no. 07/2021. The
issue relates to extension of cut-off date for determination
of experience and qualification of eligible principles in
terms of deferred advertisement. 
3. The Union Public Service Commission (in short  ‘UPSC’)
vide advertisement dated 04.04.2021 invited applications for
363  posts  of  Principals.  It  was  merely  an  indicative
advertisement, as per which last date of submission was
13.05.2021.  The  details  of  essential  qualification,
eligibility criteria etc. was mentioned to be displayed in a
separate  detailed  advertisement  on  the  UPSC’s  website.
However,  concerning  the  rise  in  COVID-19  cases,  the

--- Page 67 ---
3
advertisement was deferred  vide  online notification dated
25.04.2021,  and  the  advertisement  was  not  available.
Thereafter, UPSC re-notified the detailed advertisement on
10.07.2021, wherein following essential qualification for the
post in question were mentioned - 
“Essential Qualifications:
(A) Educational:
(i) Master’s  Degree  from  a  recognized
University/Institute,
(ii) Bachelor  of  Education  from  a  recognized
university/institute; and
(B) Experience:
Ten  years’  experience  of  teaching  (Vice
Principal / Post Graduate Teacher/ Trained Graduate
Teacher) in a recognized High School / Higher
Secondary  School  /  Senior  Secondary  School  /
Intermediate college.”
4. In  the  re-notified  advertisement,  the  last  date  of
submission of form was extended to 29.07.2021. The appellants
before this Court are the candidates who acquired eligibility
of 10 years’ experience of teaching on 29.07.2021, i.e., after
the last date of submission of form prescribed in the initial
advertisement, but prior to the last date of submission of
form as prescribed in the re-notified advertisement. 

--- Page 68 ---
4
5. Being aggrieved, the appellant-Kailash Prasad and batch
of similarly situated applicants approached CAT, which vide
interim order permitted them to participate in the selection
process.  Written  examination  was  conducted,  results  were
declared and appellants were found eligible for interview,
however, in the list as drawn, their names were excluded on
the pretext of lack of experience of 10 years as per re-
notified advertisement. Appellant challenged the list and
prayed for consideration of his case. During the pendency of
the  litigation,  results  were  declared,  keeping  13  seats
vacant.  The  result  of  appellant  was  also  withheld.
Subsequently, CAT allowed the batch of original applications
vide common order dated 15.05.2023 directing UPSC to declare
the results of the applicants and take further necessary steps
in accordance with law. On challenge before the High Court by
UPSC, the order passed by CAT was set-aside vide impugned,
hence present appeal.
6. Heard the counsels for the parties at length and perused
the  material.  It  is  not  in  dispute  that  the  initial
advertisement was notified on 24.04.2021, citing the last date

--- Page 69 ---
5
of submission of the application form as 13.05.2021. As per
the said advertisement, the crucial date for determining the
‘age limit’ shall be the closing date for submission of online
application.  So  far  as  date  of  determination  of  other
qualifications are concerned, the advertisement is silent. It
is  pertinent  to  mention  that,  the  advertisement  further
mentions  that  the  ‘detailed  advertisement  along-with
Instructions and Additional Information to candidates for
Recruitment by Selection has been displayed on Commission’s
Website’.  However,  in  wake  of  COVID-19  cases,  such
advertisement  was  deferred  the  very  next  day,  and  no
advertisement was available on the website.  
7. Subsequently, detailed advertisement was re-notified by
UPSC on 10.07.2021, extending the last date of submission to
29.07.2021. As per Clause 9(b) therein, dealing with “Other
Information/Instructions”,  the  date  of  determining  the
eligibility of all candidates in ‘every respect’ shall be the
closing date for submitting the Online Recruitment Application
on the website. It is to be noted that, on deactivation of the
portal/website after publication of the initial advertisement,
the  process  could  not  be  initiated  and  there  was  no

--- Page 70 ---
6
advertisement available on the website. After a while, a fresh
notice was issued by UPSC on 10.07.2021, whereby the same
advertisement was re-published. Since the details of said
notice are relevant, they are reproduced below for ready
reference:
“NOTICE
It is for information of all concerned that
the recruitment process, for recruitment to (363)
three hundred sixty three [208 Male & 155 Female]
vacancies  for  the  post  of  Principal  in  the
Directorate  of  Education,  Education  Department,
Government  of  NCT  of  Delhi  advertised  vide
Commission’s ‘Indicative Advertisement No. 07/2021
published in the Employment News on 24-04-2021 with
closing  date  as  13-05-2021,  has  now  been
reactivated”.  The  original  advertisement  is
reproduced below, earlier deactivated in the Month
of April, 2021 the wake of sharp rise in the
infected case of covid-19 pandemic.
2. That the Detailed Advertisement No. 07/2021
for  the  aforesaid  vacancies,  along  with
instructions  and  additional  information  to  the
candidates for recruitment by selection has been
uploaded on Commission’s website as well as ORA
module on 10-07-2021.
3. The  willing  and  eligible  candidates  may
apply on-line on or before 29-07-2021 (Print out of
the application may be taken by 23:59 hrs on 30-07-
2021).  However,  the  eligibility  and  other
conditions  as  mentioned  in  the  earlier
Advertisement No. 07/2021 published on 24-04-2021
for the vacancies remain unchanged.”
8. On perusal of the same, it is clear that the willing and
eligible  candidates  were  asked  to  apply  on  or  before

--- Page 71 ---
7
29.07.2021 and their applications may be taken up to 23.59
p.m.  on  30.07.2021.  However,  the  eligibility  and  other
conditions as mentioned in the initial advertisement No. 7/21
published on 24.04.2021 remained unchanged, meaning thereby
the eligibility of the candidates for the post in so far as
experience of ten years is concerned, shall be reckoned as on
the last date of submission of form given in the initial
advertisement. But at the same time, if the other condition
under Clause 9(b) of the advertisement is seen, which quotes
as thus:
“9(b)  –  The  date  for  determining  the
eligibility of all candidates in every respect
shall be the closing date for submitting the
Online Recruitment Application on the website
http://www.upsconline.nic.in.”
A conjoint reading of the notice appended to the detailed
advertisement and Clause 9(b) contained therein is indicative
of the fact that there is clear divergence in cut-off date for
the purpose of determining the eligibility of applicants in so
far as ten years’ experience is concerned. 
9. On  plain  reading  of  ‘Clause  9  -  Other
Information/Instructions’, it is clear that the date for
determining  the  eligibility  of  all  candidates  in  every

--- Page 72 ---
8
respect, shall be the closing date for submitting the online
recruitment application. This fact has been disputed by the
UPSC on the pretext that the said eligibility shall be
considered in terms of the initial notification issued on
24.04.2021.  In  our  considered  opinion,  such  argument  is
completely fallacious and not acceptable, for the reason that,
when the case was taken up for hearing on 27.01.2025, this
Court passed a detailed order and sought following information
from the UPSC - 
“3) During hearing, arguments and counter
arguments  were  advanced.  However,  we
want to ascertain the following facts: 
(i) What  is  the  date  of  notifying  the
advertisement on the UPSC website which
was notified in Employment Exchange on
10.07.2021?
(ii) Whether  the  subsequent  online
notification issued (at Annexure CA-4
attached  at  page  28  of  the  counter
affidavit in connected case (SLP (C) No.
700/2024)) is on the same online website
and was this published in the employment
news along with main Advertisement dated
10.07.2021 and both are uploaded on same
date?
(iii) The relevant note-sheets for prescribing
the qualification as on 13.05.2021 be
also placed.”
10. In furtherance to the aforesaid order, UPSC has filed the
affidavit annexing therein the note-sheets dated 20.04.2021

--- Page 73 ---
9
and 10.06.2021. The note-sheet dated 20.04.2021 indicates in
the wake of sharp rise in COVID-19 cases, as a precautionary
measure, it was decided to not to upload/display the detailed
advertisement on the UPSC’s website as scheduled, and it be
done on a later date in due course. Perusal of note-sheet
dated  10.06.2021  reveals  that  it  only  provided  for  re-
publication of the detailed advertisement and activation of
the portal considering the improving conditions of COVID-19
surgency. It further provided that candidates be given 20
days’ time to apply with the same eligibility conditions as
mentioned in the initial advertisement. It is pertinent to
note that the affidavit produced along-with the note-sheets do
not specify what was the reason to accept the eligibility as
on 13.05.2021 as mentioned in the initial advertisement and
not in terms of Clause 9(b) of the detailed advertisement
which provided for determination of eligibility as on the
closing  date  for  submission  of  the  online  recruitment
application on the website. 
11. Regarding query No. 2, the UPSC has stated that the
subsequent online notification was published on the same
website. As noted earlier, the UPSC’s position is that the

--- Page 74 ---
10
eligibility  cut-off  date  specified  in  the  initial
advertisement should be followed, as it was reiterated in the
detailed advertisement dated 10.07.2021. However, since no
reasons have been provided in the note-sheets for retaining
the  same  cut-off  date,  especially  when  the  detailed
advertisement could not be uploaded by UPSC after the initial
one,  we  cannot  accept  this  justification.  In  our  view,
candidates who acquired the required ten years of experience
between the last date for submitting applications under the
initial advertisement and the last date under the subsequent
detailed  advertisement  would  be  eligible  and  cannot  be
disqualified. 
12. Further, we fail to understand how the High Court has
accepted the stand of the UPSC while dealing with the issue,
especially in paragraph 15 and 23, when necessary material was
not even on record. The queries put forth by us were to
clarify the actual position and to examine the pleadings made
before the High Court. Otherwise, there was no justification
for determining a candidate’s eligibility with reference to an
earlier advertisement that was deactivated on the very next
day and for which the selection process had never commenced.

--- Page 75 ---
11
13. In view of the above discussion, we are constrained to
hold that the stand taken by the UPSC is completely misplaced
and cannot be accepted. Accordingly, the appeals are allowed.
The order of the High Court stands set-aside, restoring the
order  passed  by  Central  Administrative  Tribunal.  The
appellants who have participated in the process of selection,
their  result  be  declared  and  if  they  found  in  merit,
appointment on the seats kept vacant for them be granted. The
needful be done within a period of two months from the date of
uploading of this order.
…………………………………………………,J.
[J.K. MAHESHWARI]
…………………………………………………,J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Mr. Gautam Narayan, learned  amicus curiae  has placed his notes dated
21st April, 2026 before us, containing three issues under the heading “Part III:
Submissions”, which, according to him, would require consideration at our end. 
2. Issue  1  is  in  relation  to  condoning  the  delay  in  making  payment  of
compensation beyond the period stipulated by this Court in its judgment in
Common Cause v. Union of India 1 dated 02 nd August, 2017 and Issue No. 2
concerns  whether the  challenge  to the  termination of the  lease  and/or  the
prayer for a direction to resume mining operations can be entertained in the
present proceedings. In relation to these issues, two interlocutory applications
have been cited i.e., I.A. No.77513 of 2024 and I.A. No. 102100 of 2025.
3. Insofar  as  I.A.  No.77513  of  2024  (applicant-Kunal  Kishore  Das)  is
concerned, it is submitted that payment has been effected by him and the delay
may be condoned.
4. Mr. K. M. Nataraj, learned Additional Solicitor General, representing the
State of Orissa fairly submits that the delay can be condoned subject to liberty
1 (2017) 9 SCC 499
6

--- Page 84 ---
to the State to verify whether the payment has been effected with interest or
not.
5. Should interest be not found to have been paid, we grant liberty to the
State of Orissa to require the applicant to pay interest @ 12%. Accordingly, I.A.
No.77513 of 2024 stands disposed of.
6. In regard to I.A. No.102100 of 2025 (applicant-Shakuntala Mishra), Mr.
Narayan  has  set  out  in  his  notes  dated  21st  April,  2026  the  submissions
advanced by the applicant in support of the application reading as under:
“……. 3.3.10 The husband of the Applicant was granted a mining lease
for iron and manganese ore in an area of 33.95 Ha in Kaumula-Kouia
village of Sundergarh District vide lease deed dated 20.09.1982 for a
period  of  20  years.  (Pr.1  @  7)  On  13.09.2001,  the  lessee  filed  an
application for renewal of mining lease for 30 years over a reduced
area of 13.27 Ha. (Pr.2 @ 7) The Applicant received the first demand
notice for excess mining from the State on 16.11.2012. (Pr.4 @ 8)
Thereafter, compensation was demanded in terms of the judgment of
this Hon’ble Court dated 02.08.2017. (Pr.5-6 @ 8) During the pendency
of the recovery proceedings, the husband of the Applicant passed away
on 18.01.2022. (Pr.8 @ 9) It is the Applicant’s case that she has not
been able to pay the compensation calculated in terms of the judgment
as she could not be substituted and therefore does not have the ICMS
Code. (Pr.14-16) However, on 30.01.2024, the said mining lease was
terminated which termination was assailed by the Applicant in WP (C)
No.6585/2024. The said writ petition was disposed of on 21.03.2024
granting liberty to the Applicant to approach the Revisional Authority.
Thereafter,  the  Applicant  filed  a  Revision  Application  before  the
Ministry  of  Mines,  which  was  scheduled  on  25.04.2025,  after
completion of pleadings. (Pr.18-21 @ 14-15) …….”
7. It is submitted on behalf of the applicant that due to technical glitches at
the end of the State, the applicant could not apply for being substituted in place
of her deceased husband. Considering such submission, we grant liberty to the
State to open the portal to enable the applicant to step into the shoes of the
original lessee, who is reportedly dead. The State may verify the correctness of
the applicant’s contention and, if found correct and permitted by the rules, (i)
record the applicant’s name as lessee in place of the deceased original lessee,
and (ii) exempt her from payment of interest. The modalities prescribed in the
7

--- Page 85 ---
portal shall be followed by the applicant for substitution and for making the
requisite payment, including interest, if applicable.

regarding revival of the mining lease is pending before the Revisional Authority
(Ministry of Mines). The Revisional Authority shall be at liberty to consider the
said  revision  application  in  accordance  with  law  and  take  it  to  its  logical
conclusion. Accordingly, I.A. No. 102100 of 2025 stands disposed of.
9. List the interlocutory application i.e., I.A. No.167870/2024 (applicant-M/S

A. DIVORCE

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant approached the High Court by filing a Writ
Petition, being W.P. (C) No. 6197 of 2024 under Article 226 of the
Constitution of India, for enforcement of the contractual rights
relating to refund of the Goods and Service Tax (GST) element that
the appellant has already paid. This claim is based on Clause
2.14.A of the contract, which notes that service tax will not be
applicable in this contract, and states that any such tax, if
applicable, shall be reimbursed. The text of the provision reads as
follows:
“2.14.A  Taxes:  The  rate  quoted  by  the
Contractor shall be deemed to be inclusive of
the sales and other levies, duties, royalties &
cess,  toll,  taxes  of  Central  and  State
Governments, local bodies and authorities that
the  Contractor  will  have  to  pay  for  the
1

--- Page 106 ---
performance of this Contract. The Chhattisgarh
Housing  Board  will  perform  such  duties  in
regard to the deduction of such taxes at source
as per applicable law. Any payment claimed by
the Contractor due to any change(s) in the
existing tax structure shall not be entertained
by the Chhattisgarh Housing Board.
Note:- Service Tax will not be applicable in
this tender. if applicable then same will be
reimbursed by the C.G.H.B.”
3. The contract had an arbitration clause as well 
“1.21 ARBITRATION CLAUSE:
Except  as  otherwise  provided  in  this
contract, all questions and disputes relating
to the meaning of the specifications, designs,
drawings  and  instructions,  herein  before
mentioned as to thing whatsoever, in any way,
arising out of or relating to the contract,
designs, drawings, specifications, estimates,
concerning  the  works,  or  the  execution  or
failure to execute the same, whether arising
during the progress of the work or after the
completion or abandonment thereof, shall be
referred to the Dy. Housing Commissioner in
writing for his decision within a period of
thirty days of such occurrence. Thereupon, the
Dy. Housing Commissioner shall give his written
instructions and/or decision within a period of
sixty days of such written request. This period
can  be  extended  by  mutual  consent  of  the
parties.” 
4. The High Court examined the arbitration clause and came to the
following conclusion:
"17. One of the grounds raised by the learned
counsel for the petitioner is that Section
142(10)  of  the  CGST  Act  2017  specifically
addresses contracts entered into prior to the
implementation of GST, providing those supplies
made (supply of services) post GST shall be
taxed under the new regime. Further, the saving
provision under Section 174 of the CGST Act
safeguards  rights  and  obligations  accruing
under the erstwhile regime. Therefore, narrow
2

--- Page 107 ---
interpretation cannot be adopted to deny the
petitioner its statutory right to recover GST
in  respect  of  supplies  made  (supply  of
services) after the introduction of GST.
18. There is no dispute that clause 2.14.A of
the agreement is in relation to the taxes and
"Note" appended thereto clearly states that
service tax will not be applicable in this
tender and if applicable, then the same will be
reimbursed by the CGHB.
19. Mr. Das has drawn attention to clause 11.2
of the agreement which states that all duties
taxes  and  other  levies  payable  by  the
contractor under the contract or for any other
cause, shall be included in the total tender
price  submitted  by  the  tenderer  and  any
variation  during  execution  in  above
duties/taxes/other levies not be considered. As
such, it is for the petitioner to bear any
taxes and the petitioner cannot claim that the
respondent since has availed input tax credit,
hence, the same should be reimbursed to the
petitioner. The claim whatsoever the petitioner
is making, arises out of the terms of the
contract and any dispute with respect to the
same could be resolved under clause 1.21 which
provides for arbitration clause, however, the
same is disputed by the learned counsel for the
petitioner  stating  that  the  dispute  with
relation to tax cannot be adjudicated through
arbitration.
20. According to Mr. Rastogi, the dispute is
public  law  in  nature  and  not  a  private
contractual  claim.  We  are  in  complete
disagreement with the said submission as the
dispute itself arises out of a contract between
the petitioner and the respondent-CGHB and any
contract between two parties are restricted to
them only and not applicable universally to
all.  Any  financial  strain  or  consequential
losses to any party due to withholding of any
dues by another party cannot be a ground for
bypassing the alternate remedy available to it.
21. It is no longer res integra that disputed
question of fact cannot be decided in a writ
petition. It is needless to say that every
action of State or its instrumentality, which
3

--- Page 108 ---
is illegal, in contravention of the prescribed
procedure, unreasonable, irrational or malafide
is open to judicial review. Every executive or
administrative action of the State or other
statutory or public bodies, legally treated to
be authority, which is violative of fundamental
rights or any statute, is open to judicial
review. However, a disputed question of fact
relating to ownership of particular plot of
land, a private dispute between two persons
relating to violation of contractual agreement,
or the terms of contract by one party do not
come under the scope of judicial review.
22.  On  careful  reading  of  the  arbitration
clause, it clearly provides that 'arising out
of or relating to contract' and the claim of
the petitioner for reimbursement of the service
tax also arises out of contract and as such,
the said dispute could be resolved through
arbitration  mechanism.  The  claim  of  the
petitioner for reimbursement of the GST amount
is  frivolous  and  not  based  on  any  sound
reasons.  The  contractual  dispute  which
essentially is a money dispute and the since
the claim made by the petitioner herein is
being disputed by the respondent-CGHB, the same
cannot be adjudicated by this Court as it is
well settled that a writ   court would not come
for rescue of a party if the petition involves
disputed questions of facts. The petitioner has
the  remedy  to  approach  the  competent
jurisdictional civil court for realisation of
any amount which arises out of the contractual
obligations. The petitioner has not pursued
diligently  the  alternative  remedy  that  is
available to it.
23. As a result, this petition being devoid of
merit, is accordingly dismissed."
5. Even the review petition filed by the appellant got dismissed
by order dated 06.10.2025.
6. Heard Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, learned senior counsel appearing for
the  appellant  and  Mr.  Apoorv  Kurup,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the respondent. 
4

--- Page 109 ---
7. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion
that the dispute relating to refund on the basis of the Clause
2.14.A would not fall within the purview of the Arbitration Clause
in the Contract dated 05.02.2016. We are of the opinion that the
High Court was not justified in dismissing the Writ Petition on the
ground that there is an existing arbitration agreement between the
parties. 
8. Mr. Apoorv Kurup, learned senior counsel for the respondent
submits that Clause 2.14.A is to be interpreted in a different
manner. Mr. Apoorv Kurup, has submitted that the judgments of the
High Court in Writ Petition (C) No. 3339 of 2023 dated 29.04.2024,
as upheld by the Division Bench of the High Court in Writ Appeal
No. 350 of 2024 dated 24.06.2024, have no application to the facts
and circumstances of the case. 
9. Without expressing any opinion on the rival submissions of
Mr. Mukul Rohatgi and Mr. Apoorv Kurup, learned senior counsels, on
the merits of the case, we permit the parties to raise all
questions of law and fact before the High Court. It is for the High
Court to consider the submissions and decide the case in accordance
with law, keeping in view the scope of judicial review. It is also
clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on the merits of
the matter. 
10. In view of the above, judgment and order(s) passed by the High
Court in Writ Petition (C) No. 6197 of 2024 as well as REVP No. 320
of 2025 are set aside and the petitions are restored to their
original number for further hearing on merits. 
5

--- Page 110 ---
11. Accordingly, the appeals stand allowed to the extent indicated
above.

2026 INSC 1116

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).7249-7250/2015
ORISSA RURAL HOUSING DEVELOPMENT
CORPORATION LTD.  APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
THE ASST. COMMISSIONER OF
INCOME TAX & ORS.        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Under  the  impugned  order,  High  Court  has
dismissed  the  writ  petition  preferred  by  the
appellant, which in turn laid challenge to the order
of assessment dated 23.12.2008; the order issued by
the Commissioner of Income Tax, Bhubaneswar dated
11.03.2010 under Section 264 of the Income Tax Act,
1961 (for short ‘IT ACT’), and the order dated
15.09.2010 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax
(Appeals)-I, Bhubaneswar, with further prayer for
refund of tax collected on the ground that such
collection is without authority of law.
2. The  appellant  submitted  its  return  for
1

--- Page 114 ---
assessment year 2006-07 within time, disclosing total
loss at Rs.1,94,48,311/-. Initially, the Assessing
Officer issued notice to the appellant on 10.10.2007
under Section 143(2) of the IT Act and subsequently,
a notice under Section 142(1) dated 03.10.2008 was
issued to the appellant to produce accounts and
documents mentioned in the notice.
3. The appellant filed a petition before the
Assistant  Commissioner  of  Income  Tax,  Circle-1,
Bhubaneswar for revising the return, however, the
same was not taken account of when the Assessing
Officer passed the assessment order on 23.12.2008 and
raised a demand of Rs.7,58,33,470/- (towards tax,
surcharge  and  education  cess)  and  also  charged
interest  under  Section  234B  of  the  IT  Act  for
Rs.2,50,25,022/- totaling at Rs.10,08,58,492/-.
4. As against this order, appellant preferred a
revision before the Commissioner of Income Tax along
with  a  prayer  for  stay,  which  was  rejected  on
05.05.2009, against which appellant approached the
Commissioner of Income Tax on 27.07.2009, however,
the  revision  petition  was  dismissed  refusing  to
interfere with the assessment, on the ground that the
assessee after filing original return cannot make a
fresh claim other than by way of filing a revised
return.
2

--- Page 115 ---
5. The  appellant  thereafter,  preferred  first
appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax which
was dismissed on the ground that the appeal is not
maintainable, as the appellant has already availed
the right of filing a revision under Section 264 of
the IT Act.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant would refer
to the law laid down by this Court in Wipro Finance
Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax  1  ,   Dwarka Nath v.
Income Tax Officer  2  ,   and   Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. v.
Commissioner of Wealth Tax  3 to argue that fresh claim
can be raised before the Revisional Authority.
7. Per contra , learned counsel for the revenue
would submit that in view of law laid down by this
Court in Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax v. M/s. Om
Siddhakala Associates, Civil Appeal No. 10175 of 2026
dated 05.08.2026, it is now well settled that in the
absence of a revised return being filed in accordance
with law, the appellant cannot raise a fresh claim
before the Revisional Authority.
8. Having heard learned counsel for the parties,
we are of the considered view that the issue as to
whether a fresh claim can be raised before the
Revisional Authority without filing a revised return
1. (2022) 443 ITR 250 : 2022 SCC Online SC 675
2. (1965) 57 ITR 349 : 1965 SCC Online SC 61
3. (1970) 1 SCC 795 : 1970 (1) SCC 795
3

--- Page 116 ---
is no longer  res integra , inasmuch as in  M/s. Om
Siddhakala  Associates  (supra),  this  court  has
categorically held that when the revised return was
not submitted within time, and the assessee having
not  claimed  the  deductions  by  filing  a  revised
return,  the  same  cannot  be  availed  by  invoking
revisional jurisdiction. The following has been held
by this Court in paragraphs 4 and 5 which are
reproduced hereunder:
  “4. We are not convinced that the remand, in the facts
and circumstances of the case, was permissible. Admittedly, on
self-assessment, a return was filed by the assessee which was
processed by the Centralised Processing Centre, Income Tax
Department, Bengaluru and a notice was issued under Section
143(1) and a subsequent notice under Section 156, demanding
the outstanding tax as coming out from the returns filed on
self-assessment.  The  respondent  filed  a  revision  invoking
Section 264 of the Act before the Principal Commissioner of
Income Tax, who rejected the same on the ground that there
was unexplained delay, the tolerance limits as coming out from
Section 43CA were only prospective and that by side-wind the
attempt is to revise the return, after the period had expired, by
invoking Section 264.
5. The issue of tolerance limit was not raised in the self-
assessment  nor  was  the  assessment  revised  within  the  time
provided. The High Court, hence, fell in error, insofar as the
remand made. The assessee having not claimed the same in the
returns  filed  could have  revised the  return within  the  time
provided under the Act. When that was not done, there is no
question  of  revision under Section  264,  which would  be  an
attempt to revise the return under the garb of a revision.”
9. The reliance placed by learned counsel on
Wipro Finance Ltd. (supra), Dwarka Nath (supra) and
Sirpur  Paper  Mills  Ltd.  (supra),  is  clearly
distinguishable on facts, as in none of the matters
4

--- Page 117 ---
the issue concerning effect of non-filing of revised
return within time and in accordance with law was not
an issue. The scope of revisional jurisdiction as has
been explained in  Dwarka Nath  (supra) would not
enlarge an assessee's right to raise fresh claim
without filing revised return which has been clearly
settled  by  this  Court  in  M/s.  Om  Siddhakala
Associates (supra). 
10. The law as settled in  M/s. Om Siddhakala
Associates  (supra), has earlier been considered by
this Court in Goetze (India) Ltd. v. Commissioner of
Income-Tax  4, wherein the ratio has been laid down
that the power of the Tribunal under Section 254 of
the IT Act is to entertain for the first time a point
of law, provided the fact on the basis of which the
issue of law can be raised was before the Tribunal.
Further, the decision relied by the appellant does
not in any way relate to the power of the assessing
officer to entertain a claim or deduction otherwise
than by filing a revised return.
11. We reiterate the view taken by this Court in
Goetze (India) Ltd. (supra) and M/s. Om Siddhakala
Associates (supra), more for the reason that if the
power of the Revisional Authority is read in the
manner sought to be agitated before this Court, then
4. (2006) 284 ITR 323 : (2006) SCC Online SC 1446
5

--- Page 118 ---
there would be no end to raising any fresh claim
basing a new fact which was not before the Assessing
Officer. Allowing this, would make the assessment
procedure and the assessment order endless, and any
party can raise fresh claim before the Revisional
Authority even though there are no foundational facts
available before the Assessing Authority to consider
such claim.
12. As a matter of fact, this Court in  Shriram
Investments  v.  Commissioner  of  Income-Tax  5,  has
explained and distinguished the earlier judgment in
the matter of Wipro Finance Ltd. (supra) relied by
the appellant herein. By holding thus in paragraphs
5,  6 and 8, which are reproduced hereunder:
     “5. We have carefully considered the submissions made across the
bar. We have carefully perused the judgment of this court in the case
of    Wipro Finance Ltd.  v.    CIT    [(2022) 443 ITR 250 (SC); 2022 SCC
OnLine SC 675; (2022) 137 taxmann.com 230 (SC).] The issue which
arose before this court was not regarding the power of the Assessing
Officer to consider the claim after the revised return was barred by
time. This  court  considered  the  appellate  power  of  the  Appellate
Tribunal under section 254 of the Income-tax Act. Paragraphs 10 and
11 of the said decision in the case of Wipro Finance Ltd. v. CIT [(2022)
443  ITR  250  (SC);  2022  SCC  OnLine  SC  675;  (2022)  137
taxmann.com 230 (SC).] read thus (page 258 of 443 ITR):
“10. The learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the
Department  had  faintly  argued  that  since  the  appellant  in  its
return had taken a conscious explicit plea with regard to the part
of the claim being ascribable to capital expenditure and partly to
revenue expenditure, it was not open for the appellant to plead for
the first time before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal that the
entire claim must be treated as revenue expenditure. Further, it
was not open to the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal to entertain
such fresh claim for the first time. This submission needs to be
stated to be rejected. In the first place, the Income-tax Appellate
Tribunal was conscious about the fact that this claim was set up by
5. (2024) 468 ITR 372 : (2024) SCC Online SC 2699
6

--- Page 119 ---
the  appellant  for  the  first  time  before  it,  and  was  clearly
inconsistent and contrary to the stand taken in the return filed by
the  appellant  for  the  concerned  assessment  year  including  the
notings made by the officials of the appellant. Y et, the Income-tax
Appellate  Tribunal  entertained  the  claim  as  permissible,  even
though for the first time before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal,
in appeal under section 254 of the 1961 Act, by relying on the
dictum of this court in  National Thermal Power Co. Ltd.  v.  CIT
[(1998) 229 ITR 383 (SC); (1997) 7 SCC 489.] Further, the Income-
tax  Appellate  Tribunal  has  also  expressly  recorded  the  no
objection given by the representative of the Department, allowing
the appellant to set up the fresh claim to treat the amount declared
as  capital  expenditure  in  the  returns  (as  originally  filed),  as
revenue expenditure. As a result, the objection now taken by the
Department cannot be countenanced.
11. Learned Additional Solicitor General had placed reliance on
the decision of this court in Goetze (India) Ltd. v. CIT [(2006) 284
ITR 323 (SC); 2006 SCC OnLine SC 1446; (2006) 157 Taxman 1
(SC).] in support of the objection pressed before us that it is not
open  to  entertain  fresh  claim  before  the  Income-tax  Appellate
Tribunal.  According  to  him,  the  decision  in  National  Thermal
Power Co. Ltd.  v.  CIT  [(1998) 229 ITR 383 (SC); (1997) 7 SCC
489.] merely permits raising of a new ground concerning the claim
already  mentioned  in  the  returns  and  not  an  inconsistent  or
contrary  plea  or  a  new  claim.  We  are  not  impressed  by  this
argument. For, the observations in the decision in  Goetze (India)
Ltd. v. CIT [(2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC); 2006 SCC OnLine SC 1446;
(2006) 157 Taxman 1 (SC).] itself make it amply clear that such
limitation  would  apply  to  the  ‘assessing  authority’,  but  not
impinge  upon  the  plenary  powers  of  the  Income-tax  Appellate
Tribunal bestowed under section 254 of the Act. In other words,
this decision is of no avail to the Department.”
(emphasis added)
In  this  case,  the court  did  not  consider the question  of  the
power of the Assessing Officer to consider a claim made after a
revised  return  was  barred  by  time.  This  court  considered  the
appellate powers of the Tribunal under section 254 of the Income-
tax Act. Moreover, this was a case where the Department gave no
objection for enabling the assessee to set up a fresh claim.
6. In the case of   Goetze (India) Ltd.   v.   CIT   [(2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC);
2006 SCC OnLine SC 1446; (2006) 157 Taxman 1 (SC).], this court
held that the Assessing Officer cannot entertain any claim made by
the assessee otherwise than by following the provisions of the Income-
tax Act. In this case, there is no dispute that when a revised return
dated October 29, 1991 was filed, it was barred by limitation in terms
of section 139(5) of the Income-tax Act.
8. Coming to the decision of the Tribunal, we find that the Tribunal
has not exercised its power under section 254 of the Income-tax Act to
consider  the  claim.  Instead,  the  Tribunal  directed  the  Assessing
Officer to consider the appellant's claim.  The Assessing Officer had
no  jurisdiction  to  consider the  claim made  by  the  assessee  in  the
revised return filed after the time prescribed by section 139(5) for
filing a revised return had already expired.”
7

--- Page 120 ---
13. In our considered view, the power of the
Revisional Authority is for entertaining for the
first time a new question of law or point of law, and
not anything which is beyond the facts which were
available with the Assessing Authority.
14. In view of the above, we do not find any
substance in these appeals, which fails and are
hereby dismissed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.4868/2026
[Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.16147/2026]
ANIL KUMAR MEENA @ 
SHER SINGH MEENA  APPELLANT
                          VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN        RESPONDENT
    O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur, has declined the prayer of the appellant for grant of
bail.  His  application1 stands  dismissed  by  the  impugned
judgment and order dated 22nd May, 2026.
3. This appeal take exception to such dismissal.
4. Appellant,  figuring  as  an  accused  in  FIR  No.0010  of
2024  dated  03rd March,  2024  registered  at  Police  Station
1 S.B. Criminal Miscellaneous Regular Bail Application No.3105/2026
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.16147/2026 1

--- Page 145 ---
SOG, District ATS & SOG, Jaipur under Sections 419, 420 &
120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; Sections 4, 5 & 6 of the
Rajasthan Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means)
Act, 1992  and Section  66D of the  Information T echnology
(Amendment) Act, 2008, was arrested on 30 th March, 2024
(while already in custody in connection with FIR No.227/2022
at Police Station Bekariya, Udaipur, Rajasthan).
5. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties  and
perused  the  counter-affidavit  of  the  respondent-State  of
Rajasthan.
6. It  appears  that  upon  completion  of  investigation,
chargesheet2 qua the appellant and the co-accused  has been
filed on 01 st May, 2024 whereafter the prosecution has also
filed 16 supplementary chargesheets against a total of 150
(one  hundred  and  fifty)  accused.  Prosecution  proposes  to
record the evidence of around 180 (one hundred and eighty)
witnesses to drive home the charges against the appellant.
The trial court is yet to frame the charges. Thus, it is quite
likely that the trial, once it commences, will be a protracted
2 Charge-sheet No.07/2024
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.16147/2026 2

--- Page 146 ---
exercise. 
7. Though it further appears from the counter affidavit of
the  respondent-State  of  Rajasthan that  the  appellant is  a
habitual offender, who is standing trial in various cases, we
find  that  insofar  as  the  present  case  is  concerned,  the
maximum punishment that could be imposed if at all the
appellant  is  convicted  of  the  charges  is  three  years  of
imprisonment; and he has been in custody for  almost 30
(thirty) months.
8. That apart, it is not in dispute that some of the co-
accused have been enlarged on bail; hence, the appellant is
justified in claiming parity.
9. T aking an overall view of the matter, we are of the
considered opinion that further detention of the appellant in
custody pending trial is not necessary; and, since the appeal
deserves acceptance, the appellant may be admitted to an
order for grant of bail.
10. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.
11. Appellant  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.16147/2026 3

--- Page 147 ---
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court
and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be
imposed by it.
12. Needless to observe, if released on bail, the appellant
shall not, directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
13. In  the  event  there  is  any  breach  of  the  terms  and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty
to cancel the bail of the appellant.
14. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall  diligently

cause, that could also be seen as breach of the conditions for

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This is one of those very unfortunate litigations before this
Court pending past almost two years.
2. This litigation has something to do with a matrimonial dispute
between the husband and wife and in the process, their daughter, a
young girl aged 11 as on date is being tormented for no good
reason.
3. There are other litigations between the parties pending in the
High Court of Karnataka. We do not propose to say anything in that
regard.
4. The present petitions arise from an order dated 14.12.2023
passed in Contempt Petition No.586/2023. In fact, this Contempt
Petition is also pending before the High Court.
5. By way of the impugned order, the High Court modified its
earlier order to some extent insofar as the visitation rights, etc.
are concerned.
6. The record reveals that the husband succeeded all throughout
in so far as the custody of the minor daughter is concerned, of
course, subject to visitation rights being given to the mother.
However, one fine day, i.e., on 28.03.2024, the respondent herein
lodged a First Information Report with the Jayaprakash Nagar Police
Station, Sub-Division - Jayanagar, District Bangalore City, bearing
Crime No.0076/2024 against the petitioner herein for the offence

--- Page 175 ---
4
punishable under Sections 323, 504, 506 read with 34 of the Indian
Penal Code (for short, “the IPC”), Section 75 of the Juvenile
Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and Section 10
of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for
short, “the POCSO”), respectively.
7. Upon registration of the First Information Report, the police
started with the investigation. The investigation is still pending.
8. In the course of the investigation, medical examination was
undertaken of the victim and there are reports on record in this
regard.
9. We take notice of two orders passed by us.
(i) Order dated 08.09.2025. The same reads thus:-
“1. We heard this matter for almost half an hour. 
2. We are highly disturbed with some facts.
3. Here is a case wherein a 10-year-old girl is being
traumatised like anything in a legal battle between
her father and mother.
4. We give one last chance to the parties to sit,
talk and reach to some understanding by which the
interest of the minor daughter is protected in all
respects. The nature of the allegations levelled by
the parties against each other is something beyond
our imagination. We are inclined to put to an end all
the proceedings between the parties, civil as well as
criminal, and further work out some modalities by
which the mother has a chance to visit her daughter
once or twice in a month.
5. We are saying this because there are final orders
passed by the courts, including this Court, directing
the mother to hand over the custody of the minor
daughter to the father. Today, we are dealing with a
Contempt Petition filed by the father.
6. We humbly request both the sides to work out
something which would be in the absolute interest of
the minor daughter.
7. Post this matter on 23.09.2025 on top of the
board.

--- Page 176 ---
5
8. We make it clear that by 23.09.2025 if something
is worked out, then well and good, otherwise we shall
proceed to pass appropriate orders in accordance with
law.”
(ii) Order dated 16.10.2025. The same reads thus:-
1. This matter was fixed specially today to be taken
up in the Committee Room.
2. The parties remained present along with their
daughter Myra. First we had a brief interaction with
the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and
thereafter with the learned counsel appearing for the

3. We tried to understand the nature of the dispute

a talk with the petitioner namely ‘R’. We also had a

we briefly interacted with minor Myra also.
4. Having assessed the entire situation prevailing as
on date, more particularly, after talking to one and
all,  referred  to  above,  we  have  reached  the

to stay with her mother.

6. We will take up this matter after a period of six

7. At the same time, the proceedings under the
provisions of Protection of Children from Sexual
Offences Act, 2012 (for short “POCSO”) shall remain
stayed, as already ordered.
8. Proceedings will remain stayed.
9. This matter is to be treated as Part Heard.
10. Post this matter after six months.”
10. On 01.10.2024, this Court passed the following order:-
“1. We have interacted with the child, petitioner-’R’

6
3. At the moment we permit the child to travel to

11. We want the First Information Report lodged by the mother,
i.e., the respondent before us to be investigated in the right
direction and in accordance with law.
12. In such circumstances, we are of the view that we should
direct the CBI to takeover the investigation from the investigating
agency in-charge of the investigation as on date.

[Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.17624/2026]
RAJAN SAO   APPELLANT
                          VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND         RESPONDENT
    O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  High  Court  of  Jharkhand  at  Ranchi1,  by  the
impugned judgment and order dated 07 th April, 2026, has
dismissed the appellant’s prayer for grant of bail. 
3. Appellant, figuring as an accused in FIR No.07 of 2023
dated 18th July, 2023 registered at Police Station ATC, District
Ranchi, Jharkhand under Sections 353, 332, 307 & 120-B of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 2; Section 27 of the Arms Act,
1959  &  Sections  16,  17  &  20  of  the  Unlawful  Activities
1 High Court
2 IPC
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.17624/2026 1

--- Page 192 ---
(Prevention) Act, 1967 , was arrested on 03 rd August, 2023
[Section 333 of the IPC, added later on].
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties  and
perused  the  counter  affidavit  of  the  respondent-State  of
Jharkhand.
5. Appellant has been behind bars for almost 03 years
and 03 months. Charge-sheet was filed on 20th January, 2024.
Prosecution proposes to examine 26 (twenty six) witnesses to
drive  home  the  charges  against  the  appellant,  of  whom
evidence of only 12 (twelve) witnesses appear to have been
recorded till date. The remaining are none other than police
witnesses. Question of influencing the witnesses, if released
on bail, is thus remote. 
6. Indeed,  co-accused,  i.e.,  Boby  Saw  @  Siddharth  @
Siddharth Kumar, has been enlarged on bail vide order dated
04th August, 2025 passed by the Division Bench of the High
Court; the appellant is, thus, justified in claiming parity.
7. T aking  an  overall  view  of  the  matter,  we  find  that
further detention of the appellant in custody may not serve
any useful purpose; hence, we are inclined to accept the
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.17624/2026 2

--- Page 193 ---
appeal and grant relief as prayed by admitting the appellant
to an order for grant of bail.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.
9. Appellant  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court
and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be
imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, if released on bail, the appellant
shall not, directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
11. In  the  event  there  is  any  breach  of  the  terms  and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty
to cancel the bail of the appellant.
12. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall  diligently
attend  proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless  exempted.  If  he
abstains from attending the proceedings without justifiable
cause, that could also be seen as breach of the conditions for
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.17624/2026 3

--- Page 194 ---
grant  of  bail  and  the  trial  court  will  be  free  to  pass
appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and
grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of
the case.
14. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid
terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1.  We have heard Shri R.Basant, learned senior counsel for 
the intervenor.
2. It is submitted by him that, in view of the decision of
this Court in  All India Judges’ Association and others  Vs.
Union of India and others, (2002) 4 SCC 247, with specific
reference to paragraph 40, the present batch of matters will
have to be referred to the larger Bench. Paragraph 40 of the
judgment states as follows -
“40. Any clarification that may be required in
respect  of any  matter arising  out of  this
decision will be sought only from this Court.
The proceedings if any, for implementation of
the directions given in this judgment shall be
filed only in this Court and no other Court
shall entertain them.”
3. On a query raised by this Court if that was the case, then
the  very  writ  petition  itself  was  liable  to  have  been
dismissed as not maintainable, since the direction issued by
4

--- Page 201 ---
this Court, in the aforesaid judgment, has been violated in
framing the impugned Rules. By way of a reply, Shri R. Basant,
learned Senior Counsel, submitted that it has to be held that
the writ petition is maintainable, but this Court shall refer
the matters to the larger Bench.
4. We  are not  in a  position to  agree with  the views
expressed and submissions made by Shri R. Basant, learned
senior counsel. In fact, in the forenoon session itself, we
had suggested Shri R. Basant, learned senior counsel, qua the
preliminary objection raised, that he can make a mention of
the same before the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India. However,
Shri R. Basant, learned senior counsel, informed us that he
did not think it proper to make a mention in the afternoon
session. Thus, once again, a request has been made before this
Court to make a mention before the Hon’ble Chief Justice of
India. Accordingly, we adjourn this matter to tomorrow in
order to facilitate him to make a mention before Hon'ble the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 13990 of 2026)
MUKESH RAJAURIYA APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF U.P     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, by
the impugned order dated 27.05.2026 in Criminal Misc.
Bail Application No. 18144 of 2026 , has rejected the
appellant’s prayer for bail.
3. Appellant, is figuring as an accused in FIR No.
142 of 2025, registered at Police Station Prem Nagar,
District-Jhansi, under Sections 85, 115(2), 80(2) of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and Sections 3/4
of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
4. The facts of the case reveal that the marriage
of the appellant with the deceased was solemnized on
04.02.2022. The wife of the appellant consumed poison
1

--- Page 216 ---
and ultimately expired. Learned counsel appearing for
the appellant submits that on account of a recent
miscarriage and the demise of her father, the deceased
was suffering from depression, which led her to consume
poison.
5. It is an undisputed position that the appellant
is a government servant (a railway employee) and has
undergone incarceration for a period of approximately
one year and six months. Further, it has been brought
to the notice of this Court that proceedings before the
Trial Court stand stayed pursuant to an order passed by
the High Court in a transfer petition filed at the
instance of the complainant, resulting in no progress
in the trial.
6. Learned counsel for the respondent-State has
vehemently opposed the prayer for bail, submitting that
allegations  regarding  demand  of  dowry  have  been
levelled.
7. Having heard learned counsel for the parties,
perused  the  material  on  record,  and  taking  into
consideration the period of incarceration suffered by
the appellant as well as the fact that the trial
2

--- Page 217 ---
remains stayed under orders of the High Court, this
Court is of the opinion that the appellant is entitled
to the grant of bail.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order of
the High Court.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the
trial  court  and  subject  to  such  other  terms  and
conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts
of the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms
and conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall
be at liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
12. It is also ordered that the appellant shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending the
proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also
be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail
and the trial court will be free to pass appropriate
3

--- Page 218 ---
orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this
order and grant of bail will not be treated as findings
on the merits of the case.
14. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the
aforesaid terms.
15. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

D.NO.25293 OF 2024
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).       OF 2026
[@ D.NO.25293 OF 2024]
VARALI PROPERTIES LTD. & ANR.                      Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
MONICA AHLUWALIA & ORS.                            Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The Civil Appeals arise out of the judgment and orders of the
National  Consumer  Disputes  Redressal  Commission  (“NCDRC”)  in
Consumer  Case  No.  247  of  2020  dated  12.09.2023  and  Review
Application No. 38 of 2024 dated 16.02.2024.
3. By the orders impugned before us, the NCDRC held that the
appellants are jointly and severally liable to refund the amount
payable to respondent nos.1 and 2 (“complainants”). 
4. Brief facts leading to the filing of these appeals are that
the appellants undertook a real estate project in Gurugram, Haryana
and the complainant(s), desirous of purchasing a unit in the
project,  entered  into  a  Flat  Buyer  Agreement  (“FBA”)  dated
24.12.2013. For the purpose of financing the purchase, a tripartite
agreement dated 11.01.2014 (“Tripartite Agreement”) was entered
into, as per which, respondent no.3 agreed to extend a loan to the
1

--- Page 227 ---
D.NO.25293 OF 2024
complainant(s). Accordingly, an amount of Rs. 1,60,00,000/- was
transferred by respondent no. 3 in favour of the appellants.
Additionally, an amount of Rs. 51,60,120/- was also paid by
complainant(s) to the appellants. 
5. As per the FBA, the date for handing over of possession, after
accounting for the contractual grace period of six months was
24.06.2017. It is an admitted fact that possession was neither
handed over nor offered on the said date. It is also the case of
complainant(s) that even at the time of offering of possession of
the flat by the appellant, i.e. 31.12.2018, the property was unfit
for occupation.  
6.  In  the  above-referred  circumstances,  the  complainant(s)
approached the Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority (“HRERA”)
in April, 2019 and also invoked the jurisdiction of the NCDRC on
14.02.2020. 
7. By the order impugned before us, NCDRC held that the appellants
shall refund the entire principal amount of Rs.51,60,120/- to the
complainant(s), along with simple interest @ 9% per annum from the
date of each payment till the date of refund. Additionally, NCDRC
also directed the appellants to pay a sum of Rs. 10,000/- as cost
of litigation to the complainant(s). It may be noted that in its
judgment, NCDRC held that the liability of the appellants shall be
joint and several. The review petition filed by the appellants
against the judgment of the NCDRC dated 12.09.2023 was also
dismissed on 16.02.2024.
8. Heard Mr. Gaurav Agrawal, learned senior counsel for the
2

--- Page 228 ---
D.NO.25293 OF 2024
appellants and Mr. Senthil Jagadeesan, learned senior counsel for
the complainant(s).
9. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion
that interest of justice will be subserved if we direct the
appellants to pay a sum of Rs. 35,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Five
Lakhs) in addition to Rs. 51,60,120/- (Rupees Fifty One Lakhs Sixty
Thousand One Hundred and Twenty), which has already been deposited
by them before the NCDRC pursuant to our order dated 27.09.2024.
The payment of Rs. 35,00,000/- with the amount of Rs. 51,60,120/-
shall be treated as full and final settlement of all claims that
may exist between the parties. Ordered accordingly. 
10. We further direct that the additional amount of Rs. 35,00,000/-
shall be paid by the appellants within a period of six weeks from
today. We also direct the NCDRC to release the amount of Rs.
51,60,120/- in favour of the complainant(s) with accrued interest.
11. With these directions, the Civil Appeals stand disposed of.

N THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S) 2351-52 OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO(S) 8408-09 OF 2026)
 AMAN SINGH & ANR.                               APPELLANT(S)
                                  VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR                              RESPONDENT(S)
O R   D E R  
IA No. 276673/2026
1. On 27th April, 2026, this Court passed an order
directing the trial Courts and the High Courts to call for
reports  pertaining  to  aggravating  and  mitigating
circumstances  in  every  case  involving  an  offence
punishable with death.
2. The Court was of the opinion that, in a large
number  of  such  cases,  the  exercise  of  collecting  and
placing  on  record  the  aggravating  and  mitigating
circumstances  was  being  undertaken  only  when  the
matters reached this Court.  In terms of Paragraph 13 of
the order dated 27 th April, 2026, the direction to call for
the  aggravating  and  mitigating  circumstances  was
mandatorily made applicable to the trial Courts as well
1

--- Page 242 ---
as the High Courts.
3. The  instant  application  has  been  moved  by
National  Legal  Service  Authority  (NALSA)  seeking
clarification of the aforesaid order, particularly on the
aspect  that  the  direction  requiring  the  trial  Court  to
undertake the exercise in every case involving an offence
punishable with death is not workable and may give rise
to procedural difficulties.
4. Ms.  Rashmi  Nandakumar,  learned  counsel
representing  NALSA,  pointed  out  that  there  may  be
many  cases  wherein  the  trial  Court  may  not  even
contemplate imposing a sentence of death but as per the
directions contained in the order dated 27 th April, 2026,
the  trial  Court  would  nevertheless  be  required  to
undertake the exercise of calling for reports regarding
aggravating and mitigating circumstances in every such
case.  She  further  submitted  that,  otherwise  also,  the
trial Courts may find it very difficult to comply with the
aforesaid direction because the trial Courts may not be
possessed  with  the  requisite  resources  or  facilities  to
undertake such an extensive exercise.
2

--- Page 243 ---
5. Having  considered  the  submissions  advanced,
we  are  in  agreement  with  the  submission  of  Ms.
Nandakumar. Directions contained in Para No. 13(A) of
the order dated 27 th April, 2026 which mandate the trial
Courts to call for the report of aggravating and mitigating
circumstances, deserves to be and is hereby deleted.
6. Accordingly,  a  corrigendum be  issued  to  this
effect  and  the  corrected  copy  be  forwarded  to  all
concerned with the necessary rectification after deleting
Para No. 13(A) of the order dated 27th April, 2026.
7. IA  No.  276673/2026  stands  disposed  of
accordingly.
8. Office to proceed.

       (VIKRAM NATH)
....................,J.
   (SANDEEP MEHTA)
....................,J.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.15594/2026)
PREM ROKA      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF H.P.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Himachal
Pradesh.
3. Appellant  has  been  convicted  by  the  Court  of
Additional Sessions Judge/Special Court (CBI Court),
Shimla under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs
and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS
Act’), vide the judgment and order dated 19.09.2022 and
sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (for short,
‘R.I.’) for 10 years and to pay a fine of Rs.1,00,000/-
with a default stipulation.
4. Aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence,
1

--- Page 247 ---
appellant has preferred an appeal before the High Court
of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla (briefly ‘the High Court’
hereinafter), being Criminal Appeal No.176 of 2023.
Along with the criminal appeal, appellant filed an
application for suspension of sentence and for grant of
bail. The High Court, vide order dated 23.09.2025,
rejected the prayer of the appellant by holding as
following:
“The plea raised on behalf of appellant is
misconceived  because  maximum  sentence
prescribed for offence for which appellant
has  been  convicted  is  20  years  and  50%
thereof becomes 10 years.
Even if it is considered that being the first
time offender, he can claim the suspension of
sentence  after  expiry  of1/3rd  prescribed
sentence then also, he has yet to complete
1/3rd of 20 years and thus, we do not find
any merit in application at this stage.”
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
appellant has completed 07 years and 05 months of
custody out of the total 10 years of imprisonment.
Therefore, he may be enlarged on bail.
6. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  of  Himachal  Pradesh  submits  that
appeal is pending before the High Court. It is the
appellant who has been taking time on 04 occasions over
the last 09 months. Reliance on Section 479 of the BNS
2

--- Page 248 ---
is misplaced as that section is applicable only to
under-trials and not to convicts.
7. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, we feel that as the appellant has
already undergone incarceration for almost 07 years out
of  the  total  sentence  of  10  years,  he  should  be
released on bail. The reasoning given by the High Court
as extracted supra is erroneous inasmuch as the High
Court should have confined to the sentence imposed on
the appellant by the Trial Court and not on the maximum
sentence provided for by the statute. However, even
going  by  the  reasoning  given  by  the  High  Court,
appellant has completed 1/3rd of the maximum sentence
of 20 years.
8. That being the position, the impugned order dated
23.09.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside.
9. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
released  on  bail  forthwith  on  usual  terms  and
conditions.  Appellant  shall  co-operate  with  the
criminal appeal pending before the High Court and not
seek unnecessary adjournments.
10. At this stage, we have been informed that appellant
is a citizen of Nepal, presently residing in Delhi. We
direct the appellant not to leave the country without
intimation to the Trial Court.
3

--- Page 249 ---
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      OF 2026
(@ SLP (C) No.       OF 2026)
(@ DIARY NO. 50443 OF 2026)
STATE OF U.P. & ORS.                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
PRADEEP KUMAR SINGH                                 Respondent
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted. 
3. This appeal is directed against the order dated 24.03.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (High Court)
whereby the order of the Licensing Authority cancelling the country
liquor license for the excise year of 2018-2019 and forfeiting the
basic license fee and security deposit and the order of the
Appellate and Revisional Authority affirming the same have been
quashed and set aside.
4. Facts giving rise to filing of this appeal briefly stated are
that  the  respondent  was  allotted  a  country  liquor  shop  on
19.03.2018 in Pilikothi, District Varanasi. In pursuance of the
order of allotment, the respondent deposited a basic license fee of
Rs. 20,08,608/- and security deposit of Rs. 15,92,540/-. The
1

--- Page 274 ---
respondent also executed a rent agreement in respect of a shop at
Pilikothi Shahar, District Varanasi with the owner of the property.
5. The Excise Department conducted a survey on 12.06.2018 in
which it was found that the respondent was running a shop in
another location. The District Excise Officer on 19.07.2018 issued
a notice stating that the respondent was running country liquor
shop at a different location instead of allotted location and
directed the production of layout of shop.  On 23.07.2018, the
respondent submitted a reply to the aforesaid show cause notice.
6. The  Licensing  Authority  on  29.12.2020  passed  an  order
directing cancellation of license of the respondent country liquor
shop and forfeited the basic license fee and security deposit. The
said  order  was  affirmed  by  the  orders  dated  25.08.2021  and
11.07.2022 passed by the Appellate Authority and the Revisional
Authority, respectively.
7. Being aggrieved, the respondent challenged the same in a Writ
Petition. The learned Single Judge by an order dated 24.03.2026
allowed the Writ Petition and quashed the orders passed by the
Licensing, Appellate and Revisional Authorities. The appellant was
directed to refund the basic license fee and security amount
deposited to the respondent within a period of three months.
8. Mr. Namit Saxena, learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that the impugned order passed by the High Court is cryptic in
nature and does not assign any reasons. It is submitted that in any
case the High Court ought to have appreciated that the State is
entitled to retain the amount of Rs. 9,46,941/- that is loss on
account of the Minimum Guaranteed Quota (MGQ). 
2

--- Page 275 ---
9. On the other hand, Mr. Ashwani Kumar Dubey, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent supported the order passed by the High
Court.
10. We have considered the rival submissions and have perused the
record. On perusal of the record, we find that the order passed by
the High Court is cryptic and suffers from vice of non-application
of  mind.  The  issues  arising  out  of  the  pleadings  and  the
contentions raised before us, have not been adverted to by the High
Court in the impugned order. We are, therefore, left with no option
but to set aside the same and remit the matter to the High Court to
decide the writ petition afresh. It is clarified that this Court
has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case. We keep it
open to the parties to raise all their contentions before the High
Court and it is for the High Court to consider it. In view of the
fact that the matter has been pending since long, we request the
High Court to take it up and dispose it of expeditiously.
11. Accordingly, the appeal stands disposed of.
      …………………………………………………………………………J.
   [PAMIDIGHANTAM SRI NARASIMHA]
     …………………………………………………………………………J.
   [ALOK ARADHE]
NEW DELHI;
OCTOBER 07, 2026

                             O R D E R
1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition is granted.
2. Delay condoned.
3. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh. None has appeared on behalf of respondent No. 2,
though served.
1

--- Page 290 ---
4. The petitioner is the de facto complainant. He has
taken exception to the order dated 31.07.2025 passed by
the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter), suspending the sentence of the
second respondent and directing her release on bail till
disposal of the criminal appeal. 
5. It may be mentioned that respondent No.2 was convicted
by the learned Special Judge (Protection of Children from
Sexual Offences Act, 2012 and Scheduled Castes and the
Scheduled  Tribes  (Prevention  of  Atrocities)  Act,
1989)),/11th Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Jabalpur,  in
Sessions Trial No. 1300448 of 2014, for the offence
punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (IPC), and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for
life and to pay a fine of 10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand₹
Only) with a default stipulation as well as sentenced to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) for seven years and to
pay a fine of 5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand Only) with a₹
default stipulation, for the offence punishable under
Section 201 of the IPC, vide the judgment and order dated
18.08.2023.
6. Respondent No. 2 has assailed the aforesaid conviction
and sentence before the High Court in Criminal Appeal No.
11604 of 2023. Appeal is pending for hearing. In the
meanwhile, respondent No. 2 preferred an application for
suspension of sentence and grant of bail. By the impugned
order dated 31.07.2025, the High Court has suspended the
2

--- Page 291 ---
sentence and released the second respondent on bail till
disposal of the appeal.
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner has vehemently
argued  that  the  High  Court  was  not  justified  in
suspending the sentence of the second respondent and
enlarging her on bail, having regard to the gruesome
nature of the offence and the fact that it was an honour
killing committed by the second respondent. Trial Court
has convicted the second respondent for the offence of
committing murder of her widowed daughter-in-law. The
findings of the High Court in the impugned order is
contrary to the definitive findings arrived at by the
Trial  Court.  Further  the  High  Court  has  virtually
endorsed  the  submissions  made  on  behalf  of  second
respondent which will have an adverse impact on the
hearing of the appeal. 
8. Learned State counsel has supported the stand of the
petitioner.
9. While we take note of the fact that the second
respondent has failed to respond to the notice issued by
this Court, we are, however, conscious of the fact that
bail was granted by the High Court more than one year
ago.
10. The nature of the offence and the motive leading to
the same would definitely be considered by the High Court
while hearing the appeal, having regard to the evidence
on record and the view taken by the Trial Court.
3

--- Page 292 ---
11. We, therefore, make it clear that the observations
made by the High Court while suspending the sentence and
granting bail to the second respondent would not affect
or influence the outcome of the hearing of the appeal,
which shall be decided on its own merits.
12. We further direct that respondent No. 2 should
cooperate with the hearing of the appeal before the High
Court and should not take any unnecessary adjournments.
13. We request the High Court to hear Criminal Appeal No.
11604 of 2023 within a period of six months from the date
of mentioning before the High Court by the petitioner de
facto complainant or by the State.
14. Subject to the above, Special Leave Petition stands
disposed of.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

versus Dist. Collector Rangareddy Dist. & Ors.] held as
follows:
“The  High  court,  after  exhaustively
considering the matter has held that as far
as the petitioner was concerned, he had the
liberty  to  work  his  remedy  before  the
Special Court for relief. Therefore, it is
open  to  the  petitioner  to  approach  the
Special Court for Land Grabbing Cases and
point out that in pursuance of its decision
